messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Help with AWS
parts:
Did you want to run Rstudio server on your instance?

Otherwise using git on Linux requires nothing special other than
installing git. This will be command line git. Were you looking for a
GUI interface (by default linux machines on the cloud do not have
graphical interfaces, it's all ssh shell access).

On an Ubuntu instance:
sudo apt-get install git

Then you can you clone repos from github:
git clone https://github.com/d-rug/d-rug.github.io.git


A guide to using git command line:
https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/gitlab-basics/start-using-git.html

Thanks,

I use RStudio Desktop (not server) on a linux installation without issue.  As to a github interface, I generally use drag-and-drop on GitHub's web interface, rather than a standalone client, but the following are also available according to my google-fu:

https://www.addictivetips.com/ubuntu-linux-tips/best-github-clients-for-linux/


R studio I installed from the PPA (in /etc/apt/sources.list.d):

    deb http://ppa.launchpad.net/opencpu/rstudio/ubuntu xenial main

(if not using the same version of debian linux, the xenial and ubuntu bits may need to be altered; if using RedHat/CentOS, you'll have to use whatever the equivalent `yum` command is)


You may want to check out the Tools->Version Control menu item once you have RStudio installed...it might suit your needs.  As to AWS, there are many sub-flavors of that...  Are you looking for a google drive-like interface?  I only really have experience with AWS SQS (which is painful), but hopefully the guide that Rich sent might be helpful.


--Matt


P.S. These days you don't have to do `sudo apt-get install` ; `sudo apt install` is enough, as many of the old "apt subdashes" were rolled into the main command and apt-get is just an alias to that.

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Help with AWS
parts:
linux is case-sensitive, which is why `CD` doesn't work.  If you're expecting lowercase `cd` to return your current directory, you'll want to use

    pwd

(print/present working directory) instead. Your prompt is showing your current directory as ~, which is an alias(?) for your home directory. If the username is rstudio, `pwd` will auto-expand the ~ to /home/rstudio  The `cd` command in linux is used to change the directory

if you're not sure where your R project files are located, you can use the locate command like

    locate myFile.R

    locate myProject.Rproj

(you may need to instruct your shell to build the database for locate first - I can't remember off the top of my head how to do that).

an alternative would be something like

    find . -type f -name "myFile.R"

or like Alex has suggested, use RStudio to open the directory a bit more directly.

On Thu, 11 Jul 2019 at 14:28, Matthew D Pagel <mpa...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:

linux is case-sensitive, which is why `CD` doesn't work.  If you're expecting lowercase `cd` to return your current directory, you'll want to use

     pwd

(print/present working directory) instead. Your prompt is showing your current directory as ~, which is an alias(?) for your home directory. If the username is rstudio, `pwd` will auto-expand the ~ to /home/rstudio  The `cd` command in linux is used to change the directory

if you're not sure where your R project files are located, you can use the locate command like

     locate myFile.R

     locate myProject.Rproj

(you may need to instruct your shell to build the database for locate first - I can't remember off the top of my head how to do that).

an alternative would be something like

     find . -type f -name "myFile.R"

or like Alex has suggested, use RStudio to open the directory a bit more directly.
